The first bound follows from the ceiling in (22.471). Insert these estimates and \(N\le nU\) into (22.463). All remaining terms are bounded by \(C_aU(1+\log(S+1))\). This proves (22.474) with \(C_a\) independent of the choices made after \(C_0,R_0\). \(\square\)

Lemma 22.170. A uniformly controlled sampling basis

Assume the hypotheses of Lemma 22.151 with \(\widetilde D=(d,U/R,\ldots,U/R)\) from (22.471), and let \(B_*\) be its minimizing subgroup. Throughout the remainder of this section use \(t=x\widetilde D\) and \(D_i=\lfloor t_i\rfloor\) supplied by that lemma. These hypotheses hold if \(C_0\ge4K_g\) and (22.472) holds. Indeed \(Q_{\{0\}}\le S+1\), so the last inequality in (22.411) is precisely \(Q_{\{0\}}R^g/(C_0K_gd)\le1\).

There are constants \(b_1\ge1\), \(J\ge1\), independent of \(S,A,H,L\), such that the following dichotomy holds when \(\Lambda\ne0\).

If no \(sp\), \(1\le s\le2nS\), belongs to \(\{0\}\times B_*\), then \(Q_{B_*}=S+1\), and use an orthonormal graph basis \(f\) of \(W\). Otherwise, provided

\[ |\Lambda|<b_1^{-1}(S+1)^{-J}, \tag{22.478} \]

there is a basis \(f=(e'_1,\ldots,e'_{g-1},w)\) as in Corollary 22.155, whose first \(\dim B_*\) members span \(\operatorname{Lie}B_*\). In both cases conversion from \(f\)-jets of order \(N\) to canonical graph jets costs at most \(K_S^N\), where

\[ K_S=b_1(S+1)^J. \tag{22.479} \]

Proof. In the first case, equality of two cosets with indices between zero and \(S\) would give a forbidden positive multiple of \(p\) in the subgroup. The orthonormal change costs at most \(g^{3N/2}\), by Lemma 22.143.

In the second case write \(h=\dim B_*\le g-1\). The refined bound (22.430) gives \(\deg B_*\le C_0K_gdR^{h-g}\le C_0K_gd\). The ceiling formula for \(d\) bounds this by \(C_1(S+1)^{mg+1}\). Equation (22.429) therefore gives \(\operatorname{dist}(u,\operatorname{Lie}B_*) \ge C_2(S+1)^{-(mg+2)}\), with \(C_2>0\). Choose \(J\ge mg+2\) and \(b_1\) sufficiently large. Then (22.478) makes \(|\Lambda|\) smaller than half this distance. Equations (22.381)–(22.382) bound the inverse basis entry sum by \(C_3(S+1)^J\), because \(\sum|w_i|\le\sqrt g(\sum|u_i|^2)^{1/2}\). Include the orthonormal-to-canonical conversion by enlarging \(b_1\) once more, and apply (22.378). The forward basis remains bounded as required in Lemma 22.169. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.171. An auxiliary polynomial with small sampled jets

Assume

\[ C_0\ge\max\{4K_g,8k_g,2^{2n}(n-1)!\},\qquad X=\frac{S+1}{C_0^2}\ge4, \tag{22.480} \]

and use Lemma 22.170. Put

\[ T=\lfloor U\rfloor,\quad S_0=\lfloor X\rfloor, \quad T_0=\lfloor U/C_0^2\rfloor,\quad L_0=\log(576nC_0^2),\quad b=2n+1. \tag{22.481} \]

Fix a constant \(c\) as in Lemma 22.169, enlarged if necessary as specified in the next lemma, and set

\[ p_*=4bL_0X+4c,\qquad \delta=\frac{4k_g}{D_L C_0}(p_*+2c)U. \tag{22.482} \]

There is a nonzero section \(P\), with integer coefficients \(a_{\lambda j}\) in its field-basis expression, \(|a_{\lambda j}|\le e^\delta\), such that the following sampled divided jets have modulus at most \(e^{-p_*U}\):

  • in the first case of Lemma 22.170, all \(f\)-jets of total order at most \(2nT\) at \(su\), \(0\le s<S_0\);
  • in the second case, all \(f\)-jets of total order at most \(2nT\) with last exponent less than \(T_0\), at \(su\), \(0\le s\le2nS\).

Proof. Both are the systems of Corollary 22.152. Multiplication of a column by \(\xi_j\) does not increase the complex rank, so their matrix has rank \(\rho\) satisfying

\[ \frac\rho\nu\le\frac{k_g}{D_L C_0}=:\vartheta\le\frac18. \tag{22.483} \]

Here \(\ell=(D_0+1)\prod_i3D_i\ge \mathcal H_G(D)/n!\), and \(\nu=D_L\ell\). Entire frames do not change the rank bound: the prescribed exponent sets are closed under decreasing any exponent, so multiplication by a local unit is an invertible triangular operation on the jet values.

For \(\rho>0\), the logarithm of the left side of (22.386), with its \(p=p_*U\) and \(m=cU\), is at most \(2\rho\{\delta+(p_*+2c)U\}\). We used \(\log(1+4\rho)\le\log(1+4\nu)\le cU\). The inequality \(2\rho/(\nu-2\rho)\le4\vartheta\) and (22.482) make this at most \(\nu\delta\). Lemmas 22.144–22.145 give the required nonzero integer vector and section. For \(\rho=0\), a coordinate unit vector suffices. The coefficient and field-basis height bounds of Lemma 22.169 apply in either case. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.172. Analytic continuation in both sampling cases

There is a constant \(L_*\), depending on the fixed choices through \(S\), but independent of \(H,L\), such that the assumption \(0<|\Lambda|<e^{-L_*U}\) ensures (22.478) and the following bound for every canonical divided jet of total order at most \(nT\), at \(su\), \(0\le s\le nS\):

\[ |\text{jet}|\le K_S^{nT} \left\{2e^{\delta+cU-a_0XU} +e^{-p_*U+cU+bL_0XU}\right\}+e^{-p_*U}. \tag{22.484} \]

The constant \(c\) can be fixed before \(C_0,S\).

Proof. The fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from \(sw\) to \(su\), applied to (22.473), bounds the difference of any stated divided jet by \(s|\Lambda|e^{\delta+cU}\). Since \(\delta/U\le4k_g(p_*+2c)/C_0\), choose \(L_*\) large enough that

\[ \begin{split} L_*&\ge p_*+4k_g(p_*+2c)/C_0+c +\log(2n(S+1))+1,\\ L_*&\ge\log b_1+J\log(S+1)+1. \end{split} \tag{22.485} \]

These inequalities work for all \(U\ge1\). Every sampled jet at \(sw\) then has modulus at most \(2e^{-p_*U}\), and conversion back at the end costs at most \(e^{-p_*U}\), in the canonical directions.

In the first case, fix \(|\alpha|\le nT\) and put \(G_\alpha(z)=D_f^\alpha F(zw)/\alpha!\). Write \(w=\sum_jw_jf_j\). For \(0\le m<T\),

\[ \frac{G_\alpha^{(m)}(s)}{m!} =\sum_{|\gamma|=m}w^\gamma \binom{\alpha+\gamma}{\alpha} \frac{D_f^{\alpha+\gamma}F(sw)}{(\alpha+\gamma)!}. \tag{22.486} \]

The total order on the right is at most \((n+1)T\le2nT\). Its coefficient sum is at most \(2^{|\alpha|+m}\max(1,\sum|w_j|)^m\), because \(\binom{\alpha+\gamma}{\alpha}\le2^{|\alpha|+m}\) and the multinomial expansion dominates \(\sum_{|\gamma|=m}|w^\gamma|\). The sum \(\sum|w_j|\le\sqrt g\,|w|\) is bounded by the fixed logarithms. Enlarge the fixed \(c\) to absorb this factor and the preceding factor two. Thus the \(S_0\) sampled one-variable jets are bounded by \(e^{-p_*U+cU}\).

Apply Lemma 22.146 with \(r=2n(S+1)\) and outer radius \(8r\). The norm term is bounded by \(e^{\delta+cU}\), by (22.473). Since \(S_0\ge X/2\), \(T\ge U/2\), and \(144r/S_0\le576nC_0^2\), its conclusion gives

\[ |G_\alpha(z)|\le 2e^{\delta+cU-a_0XU} +e^{-p_*U+cU+L_0XU} \quad(|z|\le2r). \tag{22.487} \]

In particular it bounds all required \(f\)-jets at \(sw\), \(0\le s\le nS\). This includes \(w=0\); formula (22.486) then has zero terms for \(m>0\).

In the second case write \(f=(f',w)\). For a multi-index \(\alpha'\) of length \(g-1\), \(|\alpha'|\le nT\), put \(G_{\alpha'}(z)=D_{f'}^{\alpha'}F(zw)/\alpha'!\). Its divided derivative of order \(m<T_0\) is exactly the sampled jet with exponents \((\alpha',m)\). The total order is at most \(nT+T_0\le2nT\), since \(T_0\le T\). Take \(S_1=2nS+1\), \(r=2S_1\), and outer radius \(8r\) in Lemma 22.146. Here \(T_0\ge U/(2C_0^2)\), so \(S_1T_0\ge XU/2\); also \(S_1T_0\le bXU\) and \(144r/S_1=288\le e^{L_0}\). Consequently the same bound as the braces in (22.484) holds for \(G_{\alpha'}\) throughout \(|z|\le2r\). For every \(s\le nS\), its closed unit circle about \(s\) lies in that disc. Cauchy's formula bounds \(G_{\alpha'}^{(j)}(s)/j!\) by that supremum for every \(j\), including \(|\alpha'|+j\le nT\). These are precisely all the remaining \(f\)-jets. This also covers \(g=1\), when \(\alpha'\) is empty.

Finally use Lemma 22.170 to convert the \(f\)-jets to canonical graph jets at \(sw\). The conversion cost is at most \(K_S^{nT}\), since \(K_S\ge1\). Apply the earlier segment estimate in the canonical directions to return to \(su\). This proves (22.484). \(\square\)

Figure 22.12. Rectangles indicate sets of integer indices; the symbolic axes are not to scale. On the left, no positive multiple \(sp\), \(s\le2nS\), lies in the minimizing subgroup. Few nodes carry every jet through order \(2nT\). On the right, many nodes carry only low orders in the last direction \(w\); the panel fixes all other exponents at zero. The proof of Lemma 22.172 uses every \(|\alpha'|\le nT\), recovering last orders through \(nT-|\alpha'|\) by Cauchy's formula. Both arguments bound all required jets at the target nodes \(0\le s\le nS\).

Theorem 22.173. A fixed-data coefficient-height estimate

For the fixed elliptic curves, algebraic points, logarithms and degree bound above, there is \(C>0\) such that every algebraic tuple with \([K(u_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g):\mathbf Q]\le D_*\) and \(\Lambda=u_0-\sum_i\beta_i u_i\ne0\) satisfies

\[ \log|\Lambda|\ge -C\{h(1:u_0:\beta_1:\cdots:\beta_g)+1\}. \tag{22.488} \]

The constant may depend on the fixed logarithms and their points. The assertion is not a numerical bound uniform in varying elliptic curves or varying points.

Proof. First retain the normalization and nonzero \(\beta_i\) used above. Fix the common constant \(c\) in Lemmas 22.169 and 22.172. Choose \(C_0\) satisfying (22.480) and

\[ \frac{16k_gb\log(576nC_0^2)}{C_0}\le\frac{a_0}{16}. \tag{22.489} \]

Such a choice exists since \(\log C_0/C_0\to0\). Now fix \(R_0,m,b_0,C_a,b_1,J\) from Lemmas 22.169–22.170. Choose the integer \(S\) so large that \(X=(S+1)/C_0^2\ge4\) and

\[ \frac{24k_gc}{C_0}\le\frac{a_0X}{16},\qquad c+n\log K_S+C_a(1+\log(S+1))+\log4 \le\frac{a_0X}{8}. \tag{22.490} \]

The left side of the second inequality grows at most logarithmically in \(S\), whereas its right side grows linearly. This proves existence. These limiting comparisons need no unproved rate assertion: \(\log t=\int_1^t dx/x\le2\sqrt t\) for \(t\ge1\) already suffices. Finally define \(d,R\), choose a fixed \(A\) satisfying (22.472), and set \(U=A(H+1)\). Every choice before \(U\) is independent of the variable coefficient tuple and of \(H\).

Apply Lemma 22.151 to obtain the positive integer degrees \(D_i\). Its subgroup may depend on the coefficient tuple, but all estimates in Lemma 22.170 are uniform. Fix \(L_*\) by (22.485). Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(0<|\Lambda|<e^{-L_*U}\). The dichotomy supplies the appropriate basis, and Lemma 22.171 supplies a nonzero auxiliary section. By (22.482), (22.489) and the first part of (22.490),

\[ \frac{D_L\delta}{U} =\frac{16k_gbL_0}{C_0}X+\frac{24k_gc}{C_0} \le\frac{a_0X}{8}. \tag{22.491} \]

Corollary 22.161 supplies a nonzero canonical jet at some \(sp\), \(0\le s\le nS\), of order at most \(nT\). At that point take its least nonzero total order and a nonzero coefficient \(f_\alpha\) of that order. Entire frames preserve the order of a section, so Lemma 22.169 applies to this very coefficient. Equations (22.474), (22.490) and (22.491) give

\[ |f_\alpha|\ge e^{-a_0XU/4}. \tag{22.492} \]

On the other hand, \(T\le U\), \(\delta\le D_L\delta\), and the second inequality in (22.490) bound the first term of (22.484) by \(2e^{-3a_0XU/4}\). Its second term is at most \(e^{-(3bL_0-a_0/8)XU}\), using \(p_*=4bL_0X+4c\). Since \(bL_0\ge a_0\), this is at most \(e^{-23a_0XU/8}\). The last term is at most \(e^{-4a_0XU}\). Their sum is at most \(4e^{-3a_0XU/4}\). Since (22.490) also gives \(\log4\le a_0X/8\) and \(U\ge1\),

\[ |f_\alpha|\le e^{-5a_0XU/8}<e^{-a_0XU/4}, \tag{22.493} \]

contradicting (22.492). Thus the normalized form satisfies \(\log|\Lambda|\ge-L_*A(H+1)\).

For an arbitrary tuple, omit its zero \(\beta_i\). If none remain, Lemma 22.47 gives the assertion directly. Otherwise normalize by Lemma 22.141. The normalized height is at most the original one, and the normalization scalar has logarithm at least \(-D_*H\). Add this loss to the preceding estimate. There are finitely many nonempty subsets of the fixed elliptic factors; take the maximum of their constants and \(D_*\). This proves (22.488) for every tuple. \(\square\)

Exercise 22.174. Rational approximation to a real elliptic period

Let \(\omega>0\) be a nonzero real period of \(y^2=x^3-x\) for \(dx/(2y)\). Show that there are constants \(c_\omega>0\) and \(\mu_\omega>0\) such that

\[ \left|\omega-\frac ab\right| \ge c_\omega |b|^{-\mu_\omega} \qquad(a,b\in\mathbf Z,\ b\ne0). \tag{22.494} \]

No explicit numerical value of \(\mu_\omega\) is asserted.

Solution. The transcendence of the nonzero period was proved in Proposition 22.9 using Theorem 22.64, so \(a-b\omega\ne0\). Apply Theorem 22.173 with the fixed point equal to the identity and its fixed logarithm equal to \(\omega\). For \(B=\max(2,|a|,|b|)\), the coefficient height is at most \(\log B\), and \(|a-b\omega|\ge e^{-C}B^{-C}\). If \(|\omega-a/b|<1\), then \(|a|\le(\omega+1)|b|\) and \(B\le(\omega+2)|b|\). Dividing the lower bound by \(|b|\) proves (22.494) with \(\mu_\omega=C+1\) and \(c_\omega=\min(1,e^{-C}(\omega+2)^{-C})\). If \(|\omega-a/b|\ge1\), the same inequality follows from \(|b|\ge1\) and \(c_\omega\le1\).

For comparison, the freely accessible author version of É. Gaudron's Mesures d'indépendance linéaire de logarithmes dans un groupe algébrique commutatif, Theorem 3 and Sections 6.6–6.13, gives a general commutative-group estimate with the same linear coefficient-height dependence when the group, nonadditive points, logarithms and field degree are fixed. The proof above treats the product of the specified plane cubic models and makes both sampling cases explicit.

Explicit growth of elliptic homogeneous coordinates

Let \(\tau\) lie in the upper half-plane, put \(y=\operatorname{Im}\tau\), and write \(L_\tau=\mathbf Z+\tau\mathbf Z\). We use the normalization \(\wp_\tau(z)=z^{-2}+O(z^2)\). Its construction, periodicity, Laurent expansion and cubic equation are proved in Weierstrass functions, elliptic values and periods, Propositions 8.1–8.2. The following estimates make the dependence on the lattice explicit. All terminating decimals in the inequalities below denote exact rational numbers.

Proposition 22.175. An entire denominator and its transformation law

Put \(q=e^{2\pi i\tau}\), \(w=e^{2\pi iz}\), and define

\[ \phi_\tau(z)=\frac{w-1}{2\pi i} \prod_{r=1}^{\infty} \frac{(1-q^rw)(1-q^r/w)}{(1-q^r)^2}. \tag{22.495} \]

This is entire, has exactly the simple zeros \(L_\tau\), and \(\phi_\tau'(0)=1\). For integers \(m,n\),

\[ \begin{split} \phi_\tau(z+m+n\tau)&=A_n(z)\phi_\tau(z),\\ A_n(z)&=(-1)^n \exp\{-2\pi inz-\pi in(n-1)\tau\},\\ \phi_\tau(-z)&=-e^{-2\pi iz}\phi_\tau(z). \end{split} \tag{22.496} \]

Proof. On any compact set of \(z\)'s, both \(|w|\) and \(|w|^{-1}\) are bounded. The sum of the deviations of the product factors from one is consequently bounded by a constant times \(\sum_r|q|^r\). For a tail with deviations at most \(1/2\), the power series for \(\log(1+u)\) converges uniformly and absolutely. Its sum exponentiates to a holomorphic, nowhere-zero tail product. The finitely many other factors show normal convergence, holomorphy and the asserted zeros. Each zero belongs to exactly one numerator factor or to \(w-1\); that factor has a simple zero. At zero all product factors equal one, and \((w-1)/(2\pi i)=z+O(z^2)\).

Period one is immediate. Substituting \(qw\) for \(w\) and shifting the indices in the two numerator products gives \(\phi_\tau(z+\tau)=-w^{-1}\phi_\tau(z)\). The identity initially holds away from the zeros and extends across them by continuity. Iteration gives (22.496) for positive \(n\); solving the same identity backwards gives it for negative \(n\). Replacing \(w\) by \(w^{-1}\) interchanges the two products and multiplies their prefactor by \(-w^{-1}\). This proves the reflection formula. \(\square\)

Proposition 22.176. Fourier and half-period identities

Away from \(L_\tau\), the normally convergent expression

\[ \wp_\tau(z)=-4\pi^2\left\{ \frac1{12}+\frac{w}{(w-1)^2} +\sum_{r\ge1}\left[ \frac{wq^r}{(1-wq^r)^2} +\frac{w^{-1}q^r}{(1-w^{-1}q^r)^2} -\frac{2q^r}{(1-q^r)^2}\right]\right\} \tag{22.497} \]

holds. For \(v\notin L_\tau\),

\[ \frac{\phi_\tau(z+v)\phi_\tau(z-v)}{\phi_\tau(z)^2} =e^{-2\pi iv}\phi_\tau(v)^2 \bigl(\wp_\tau(v)-\wp_\tau(z)\bigr). \tag{22.498} \]

In particular, with \(e_1=\wp_\tau(1/2)\) and \(G(z)=\phi_\tau(z+1/2)\phi_\tau(z-1/2)/\phi_\tau(1/2)^2\),

\[ \phi_\tau^2\wp_\tau=e_1\phi_\tau^2+G, \qquad \phi_\tau^3\wp_\tau'=\phi_\tau G'-2\phi_\tau'G. \tag{22.499} \]

The products on the left extend holomorphically across the lattice.

Proof. Logarithmic differentiation of (22.495) is valid on compact sets away from its zeros: the differentiated tails are still bounded by a convergent geometric series. The meromorphic function \(F=-(\phi_\tau'/\phi_\tau)'\) is periodic by (22.496). At every simple zero of \(\phi_\tau\) it has principal part \((z-\lambda)^{-2}\), with no simple-pole term. Thus \(F-\wp_\tau\) is entire and periodic, hence constant. Indeed, it is bounded on a closed fundamental parallelogram and therefore on the plane; Cauchy's derivative estimate on circles of radius tending to infinity makes its derivative zero.

The differentiated product gives the expression in braces in (22.497) without its constant \(1/12\) and without the last summand \(-2q^r/(1-q^r)^2\). Since

\[ \frac{w}{(w-1)^2} =-\frac1{4\sin^2(\pi z)} =-\frac1{4\pi^2z^2}-\frac1{12}+O(z^2), \tag{22.500} \]

the constant Laurent coefficient of \(F\) is \(\pi^2/3-8\pi^2\sum_{r\ge1}q^r/(1-q^r)^2\). Subtracting it yields (22.497), because the constant coefficient of \(\wp_\tau\) is zero.

The left side of (22.498) is periodic by the transformation law and even by the reflection formula. Its only possible poles are double poles at the lattice, and the coefficient at zero is \(\phi_\tau(v)\phi_\tau(-v) =-e^{-2\pi iv}\phi_\tau(v)^2\). Evenness excludes a simple-pole term. Subtract the right side of (22.498). All poles cancel, so the difference is constant. Its value at \(z=v\) is zero. This proves the identity. For \(v=1/2\), \(e^{-2\pi iv}=-1\), which gives the first formula (22.499). Differentiate it and multiply by \(\phi_\tau\); the terms containing \(e_1\) cancel and give the second. The pole orders of \(\wp\) and \(\wp'\) are two and three, so the stated products are entire. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.177. Rational bounds for the numerical constants

Suppose \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\), and put \(Q=e^{-2\pi y}\). Then

\[ Q<\frac1{230},\qquad \sqrt Q<\frac{33}{500},\qquad e^{-\pi y/4}<\frac{507}{1000}. \tag{22.501} \]

The following bounds will be used:

\[ \begin{split} \frac{2Q}{(1-Q)^2}+\frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{1-Q}&<\frac{19}{250},\\ e^{19/250}&<1.079,\\ \frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{(1-Q)(1-\sqrt Q)}&<0.072. \end{split} \tag{22.502} \]

Proof. Here are finite rational certificates, including the bounds for \(\pi\) used in them. For \(0<t<1\), let \(a_N(t)=\sum_{j=0}^N(-1)^jt^{2j+1}/(2j+1)\). Integration of the finite geometric identity for \(1/(1+t^2)\) shows that \(a_5(t)<\arctan t<a_4(t)\). The tangent addition formula and the fact that both angles are in \((0,\pi/2)\) give \(\arctan(1/2)+\arctan(1/3)=\pi/4\). Direct rational comparison therefore gives

\[ \frac{157}{50} <4\{a_5(1/2)+a_5(1/3)\}<\pi <4\{a_4(1/2)+a_4(1/3)\}<\frac{22}{7}. \tag{22.503} \]

Also \((433/250)^2<3\). Put \(x=67981/12500 =(157/50)(433/250)\). With \(T_N(t)=\sum_{j=0}^Nt^j/j!\), rational arithmetic gives

\[ T_{30}(x)>230,\quad T_{25}(x/2)>500/33,\quad T_{20}(x/8)>1000/507. \tag{22.504} \]

Every omitted term in the exponential series is positive, so (22.503)–(22.504) imply (22.501). These rational tests can also be performed without large denominators by multiplying each inequality by the corresponding positive power of \(12500\) and by \(30!\).

The first and third expressions in (22.502) increase with both \(Q\) and \(\sqrt Q\) in \((0,1)\). Substitution of \(1/230\) and \(33/500\) gives the stated rational inequalities. For the exponential, put \(b=19/250\). From the twelfth term onwards, successive term ratios are at most \(b/13\). Hence

\[ e^b\le T_{11}(b)+\frac{b^{12}}{12!}\frac1{1-b/13} <\frac{1079}{1000}. \tag{22.505} \]

The last comparison is rational. These arguments prove strict upper bounds, rather than decimal approximations to the constants. \(\square\)

Proposition 22.178. Estimates on a fundamental cell

Assume \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\). For \(z_0=s+t\tau\) with \(|s|,|t|\le1/2\), set

\[ J_\tau(z)=\frac{(\operatorname{Im}z)^2}{y} -\operatorname{Im}z+\frac y4, \qquad J_\tau(z_0)=y(t-1/2)^2. \tag{22.506} \]

Then

\[ \begin{split} |\phi_\tau(z_0)|&<0.26e^{\pi J_\tau(z_0)},\\ |\phi_\tau'(z_0)|&<1.197e^{\pi J_\tau(z_0)},\\ |\phi_\tau(1/2)|&>0.312,\qquad |\wp_\tau(1/2)|<7.3. \end{split} \tag{22.507} \]

The first two estimates also hold at \(z_0+1/2\) and \(z_0-1/2\), with the same value of \(J_\tau\).

Proof. Write \(a=|e^{2\pi iz_0}|=Q^t\). Thus both \(aQ\) and \(a^{-1}Q\) are at most \(\sqrt Q\). The absolute value of the product part of (22.495) is at most

\[ P=\prod_{r\ge1} \frac{(1+aQ^r)(1+a^{-1}Q^r)}{(1-Q^r)^2} \le\exp\left\{\frac{2Q}{(1-Q)^2} +\frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{1-Q}\right\}<1.079. \tag{22.508} \]

Indeed, \(\log(1+u)\le u\) and \(-\log(1-u)\le u/(1-u)\) follow by integrating their respective derivatives. Also \(a+a^{-1}\le Q^{-1/2}+Q^{1/2}\): the even function \(Q^t+Q^{-t}\) increases with \(|t|\). Summing the geometric majorants proves (22.508).

Differentiate the numerator factors in (22.495). The sum of the absolute logarithmic derivatives of the product, divided by \(2\pi\), is bounded by

\[ S=\sum_{r\ge1}\left\{ \frac{aQ^r}{1-aQ^r}+\frac{a^{-1}Q^r}{1-a^{-1}Q^r}\right\} \le\frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{(1-Q)(1-\sqrt Q)}<0.072. \tag{22.509} \]

No numerator factor vanishes in this cell: its modulus parameter is at most \(\sqrt Q<1\). Direct differentiation of the prefactor, including at its zeros, now yields

\[ |\phi_\tau(z_0)|<0.172(1+a),\qquad |\phi_\tau'(z_0)|<1.079\{a+0.072(1+a)\}. \tag{22.510} \]

Here \(1.079/(2\pi)<0.172\) by (22.503).

Both

\[ \begin{split} a e^{-\pi J_\tau(z_0)}&=e^{-\pi y(t+1/2)^2}\le1,\\ (1+a)e^{-\pi J_\tau(z_0)} &=e^{-\pi y(t-1/2)^2}+e^{-\pi y(t+1/2)^2}<1.507 \end{split} \tag{22.511} \]

hold: at least one of \(|t-1/2|,|t+1/2|\) is at least \(1/2\). The other exponential is at most one, and (22.501) bounds the first by \(0.507\). The rational inequalities \(0.172\cdot1.507<0.26\) and \(1.079(1+0.072\cdot1.507)<1.197\) prove the first two assertions of (22.507). Integer real translations reduce \(s\pm1/2\) to the same cell and leave both \(J_\tau\) and \(\phi_\tau,\phi_\tau'\) unchanged.

At \(z=1/2\), formula (22.495) and the reverse triangle inequality give

\[ |\phi_\tau(1/2)|\ge\frac1\pi \prod_{r\ge1}\left(\frac{1-Q^r}{1+Q^r}\right)^2 \ge\frac1\pi e^{-4Q/(1-Q)^2} >\frac7{22}\left(1-\frac{920}{52441}\right)>0.312. \tag{22.512} \]

For the middle inequality use \(\log(1-u)-\log(1+u)\ge-2u/(1-u)\), then sum and use \(1-Q^r\ge1-Q\). For the next one use \(e^{-v}\ge1-v\) and (22.501),(22.503).

Finally set \(w=-1\) in (22.497). The constant part has modulus \(2\pi^2/3\). The remaining four terms for each \(r\) have total modulus at most \(16\pi^2Q^r/(1-Q^r)^2\). Consequently

\[ |\wp_\tau(1/2)|\le\frac{2\pi^2}{3} +\frac{16\pi^2Q}{(1-Q)^3}<7.3, \tag{22.513} \]

by substituting \(\pi<22/7\) and \(Q<1/230\). \(\square\)

Theorem 22.179. A global Gaussian upper bound

For \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\), the entire tuple

\[ \Phi_\tau(z)= \bigl(\phi_\tau(z)^3,\; \phi_\tau(z)^3\wp_\tau(z),\; \phi_\tau(z)^3\wp_\tau'(z)\bigr) \tag{22.514} \]

has no common zero and represents \([1:\wp_\tau:\wp_\tau']\). With \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) the maximum coordinate norm,

\[ \|\Phi_\tau(z)\|_\infty \le3.33\exp\left\{3\pi\left( \frac{(\operatorname{Im}z)^2}{y} -\operatorname{Im}z+\frac y4\right)\right\}. \tag{22.515} \]

In particular it is at most \(3.33\exp\{3\pi((\operatorname{Im}z)^2/y +|\operatorname{Im}z|+y/4)\}\).

For a scaled lattice \(L=\omega_1 L_\tau\), \(\omega_1\ne0\), set \(\phi_L(z)=\omega_1\phi_\tau(z/\omega_1)\) and form \(\Phi_L=(\phi_L^3,\phi_L^3\wp_L,\phi_L^3\wp_L')\). Then

\[ \|\Phi_L(z)\|_\infty \le3.33\max\{1,|\omega_1|^3\} e^{3\pi J_\tau(z/\omega_1)}. \tag{22.516} \]

Proof. First work on the cell of Proposition 22.178 and abbreviate \(J=J_\tau(z_0)\). By (22.499),(22.507), the three coordinates have respective upper bounds

\[ \begin{split} 0.26^3 e^{3\pi J}&<0.0176e^{3\pi J},\\ 0.26^3(7.3+0.312^{-2})e^{3\pi J}&<0.309e^{3\pi J},\\ \frac{4\cdot0.26^2\cdot1.197}{0.312^2}e^{3\pi J} &=3.325e^{3\pi J}<3.33e^{3\pi J}. \end{split} \tag{22.517} \]

In the third line, \(\phi G'\) supplies two summands and \(2\phi'G\) supplies two more, each bounded by \(0.26^2\cdot1.197e^{3\pi J}/0.312^2\). These are finite rational comparisons.

Every \(z\) can be written \(z=z_0+m+n\tau\) with \(z_0\) in that cell. Periodicity of \(\wp\) and \(\wp'\) and (22.496) give the exact scalar law

\[ \Phi_\tau(z)=A_n(z_0)^3\Phi_\tau(z_0),\qquad \log|A_n(z_0)|=\pi\{2n\operatorname{Im}z_0+(n^2-n)y\}. \tag{22.518} \]

The expression in braces plus \(J_\tau(z_0)\) is exactly \(J_\tau(z)\). Multiplication of (22.517) by \(|A_n(z_0)|^3\) proves (22.515) globally. At zero, \(\phi=z+O(z^2)\), \(\wp=z^{-2}+O(z^2)\) and \(\wp'=-2z^{-3}+O(z)\); thus the tuple is \((0,0,-2)\). Its scalar transformation law proves nonvanishing at every lattice point. Away from the lattice its first coordinate is nonzero.

Changing variables in the defining lattice series gives \(\wp_L(z)=\omega_1^{-2}\wp_\tau(z/\omega_1)\) and \(\wp_L'(z)=\omega_1^{-3}\wp_\tau'(z/\omega_1)\). Thus the three coordinates of \(\Phi_L\) are those of \(\Phi_\tau(z/\omega_1)\) multiplied by \(\omega_1^3,\omega_1,1\), respectively. Since \(\max\{1,|\omega_1|,|\omega_1|^3\} =\max\{1,|\omega_1|^3\}\), (22.516) follows. \(\square\)

Figure 22.13. For \(\tau=i\), the blue curve shows numerically sampled values of \(\log\|\Phi_i(1/3+it)\|_\infty\). The orange curve is the proved upper bound \(\log(3.33)+3\pi(t-1/2)^2\). Its centre at \(t=1/2\) comes from the chosen denominator's transformation law. The samples illustrate (22.515); its proof is independent of them.

Exercise 22.180. Differentiation and lattice translation

Find the transformation law for \(\phi_\tau'\). Explain why the estimate for this derivative in (22.507) cannot simply be translated with the scalar \(A_n\). For \(\tau=i\), show that there is no constant \(C\) such that

\[ |\phi_i'(z)|\le C e^{\pi J_i(z)}\qquad(z\in\mathbf C). \tag{22.519} \]

Why does this not obstruct the bound for the tuple \(\Phi_i\)?

Solution. Differentiate (22.496):

\[ \phi_\tau'(z+m+n\tau)= A_n(z)\{\phi_\tau'(z)-2\pi in\phi_\tau(z)\}. \tag{22.520} \]

At \(z=1/3\), \(\phi_i(z)\ne0\). Dividing the absolute value of (22.520) by \(e^{\pi J_i(z+ni)}\) gives exactly

\[ e^{-\pi/4} |\phi_i'(1/3)-2\pi in\phi_i(1/3)|, \tag{22.521} \]

which tends to infinity with \(|n|\), by the reverse triangle inequality. This disproves (22.519) for every fixed \(C\). In contrast, \(\wp\) and \(\wp'\) are periodic. Their products with \(\phi^3\) therefore obey (22.518) with no derivative term. One first estimates those complete products on a fundamental cell, then translates them. Formula (22.499) is only needed for the cell estimate. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.181. Product lower bounds on the cell

Keep the cell and notation of Proposition 22.178. Write \(P_\tau(z)\) for the product in (22.495), without its prefactor. Then

\[ |P_\tau(z_0)|>0.919,\qquad |\phi_\tau(z_0)|\ge0.146|w-1|. \tag{22.522} \]

The second inequality is strict when \(w\ne1\). For \(g(b)=b(1+b)/(1-b)^3\), one also has

\[ \begin{split} \sum_{r\ge1}\{|g(wq^r)|+|g(q^r/w)|\}&<\frac1{10},\\ \frac1{12}+\sum_{r\ge1}\left\{ \frac{aQ^r}{(1-aQ^r)^2} +\frac{a^{-1}Q^r}{(1-a^{-1}Q^r)^2} +\frac{2Q^r}{(1-Q^r)^2}\right\}&<\frac15. \end{split} \tag{22.523} \]

Proof. The reverse triangle inequality and \(\log(1-u)\ge-u/(1-u)\), \(\log(1+u)\le u\), give

\[ \log|P_\tau(z_0)|\ge -\frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{(1-Q)(1-\sqrt Q)} -\frac{2Q}{1-Q}>-0.081. \tag{22.524} \]

The last inequality follows from (22.501)–(22.502), since \(0.072+2/229<0.081\). Thus \(|P_\tau(z_0)|>e^{-0.081}\ge1-0.081=0.919\). As \(0.919\cdot7/44>0.146\), (22.503) proves (22.522).

For \(|b|\le h=\sqrt Q\), \(|g(b)|\le |b|(1+h)/(1-h)^3\). Summing \(|wq^r|+|q^r/w|\) therefore bounds the first expression in (22.523) by

\[ \frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{1-Q} \frac{1+\sqrt Q}{(1-\sqrt Q)^3}<\frac1{10}. \tag{22.525} \]

Similarly the second expression is at most

\[ \frac1{12} +\frac{\sqrt Q(1+Q)}{(1-Q)(1-\sqrt Q)^2} +\frac{2Q}{(1-Q)^3}<\frac15. \tag{22.526} \]

In both cases the expressions increase with \(Q\) and \(\sqrt Q\). Substitute \(1/230\) and \(33/500\) to obtain the displayed strict rational inequalities. \(\square\)

Theorem 22.182. An explicit lower bound for the entire tuple

For every \(z\in\mathbf C\), \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\),

\[ \begin{split} \|\Phi_\tau(z)\|_\infty &\ge 0.073^3 e^{3\pi(J_\tau(z)-y)}\\ &\ge 7\cdot10^{-4} \exp\left\{\pi\left( -2.51y-3|\operatorname{Im}z| +\frac{3(\operatorname{Im}z)^2}{y}\right)\right\}. \end{split} \tag{22.527} \]

For a scaled lattice as in Theorem 22.179,

\[ \|\Phi_L(z)\|_\infty \ge\min\{1,|\omega_1|^3\}\,0.073^3 e^{3\pi(J_\tau(z/\omega_1)-y)}. \tag{22.528} \]

Proof. First prove that the tuple norm on the cell is at least \(c=0.073^3\). If \(|w-1|\ge1/2\), (22.522) gives \(|\phi_\tau|\ge0.073\), so its first coordinate suffices. Suppose instead \(|w-1|<1/2\). Differentiating (22.497) gives

\[ \phi_\tau(z_0)^3\wp_\tau'(z_0) =P_\tau(z_0)^3\left\{ -w(1+w)+(w-1)^3 \sum_{r\ge1}\bigl(g(wq^r)-g(q^r/w)\bigr)\right\}. \tag{22.529} \]

Multiplication removes the pole, so this identity also holds when \(w=1\). In the present case \(|w|>1/2\) and \(|1+w|>3/2\). Lemma 22.181 gives the lower bound \(0.919^3(3/4-1/80)>0.073^3\) for the absolute value in (22.529). This proves the cell bound, including the lattice point.

Write \(z=z_0+m+n\tau\) as before. Since \(J_\tau(z_0)=y(t-1/2)^2\le y\), (22.518) gives the first inequality in (22.527). If \(v=\operatorname{Im}z\), its exponent minus the second exponent is \(\pi\{0.26y+3(|v|-v)\}\ge0.26\pi y\). This is larger than \(b=(13/100)(67981/12500)\), by (22.503) and \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\). The rational comparison \(0.073^3(1+b+b^2/2)>7\cdot10^{-4}\), together with \(e^b\ge1+b+b^2/2\), proves the second inequality. Finally the three scaling factors from (22.516) have minimum \(\min\{1,|\omega_1|^3\}\). This proves (22.528). \(\square\)

Proposition 22.183. A lower bound for the denominator itself

For \(z\notin L_\tau\), \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\),

\[ |\phi_\tau(z)|(1+|\wp_\tau(z)|) \ge0.073e^{-2\pi|\operatorname{Im}z|} \ge10^{-2}e^{-\pi y/2-4\pi|\operatorname{Im}z|}. \tag{22.530} \]

For the scaled lattice \(L=\omega_1L_\tau\) and \(z\notin L\),

\[ |\phi_L(z)|(1+|\wp_L(z)|) \ge\frac{0.073|\omega_1|}{\max\{1,|\omega_1|^2\}} e^{-2\pi|\operatorname{Im}(z/\omega_1)|}. \tag{22.531} \]

Proof. On the cell, if \(d=|w-1|\ge1/2\), the estimate \(|\phi_\tau|\ge0.073\) suffices. If \(0<d<1/2\), isolate the term \(w/(w-1)^2\) in (22.497) and use (22.523). Since \(|w|>1/2\), the reverse triangle inequality gives

\[ |\wp_\tau(z_0)| >4\pi^2\left(\frac1{2d^2}-\frac15\right) >\frac{4\pi^2\cdot0.45}{d^2}. \tag{22.532} \]

Multiply by \(|\phi_\tau(z_0)|>0.146d\). The resulting bound is greater than \(8(157/50)^2\cdot0.45\cdot0.146>0.073\), because \(d<1/2\). Thus the first product in (22.530) is at least \(0.073\) throughout the cell away from the lattice.

For the translation \(z=z_0+m+n\tau\), set \(M/y=n^2-n+2nt\), so that \(|A_n(z_0)|=e^{\pi M}\). If \(n\le0\), then \(M/y\ge n^2\ge0\); if \(n\ge2\), then \(M/y\ge n(n-2)\ge0\). For \(n=0\) it is zero. The remaining case is \(n=1\). If \(t\ge0\), again \(M\ge0\). If \(-1/2\le t<0\), then \(M=2ty\ge-2(1+t)y=-2|\operatorname{Im}z|\). Thus \(M\ge-2|\operatorname{Im}z|\) in every case. Periodicity of \(\wp\) and (22.496) prove the first inequality in (22.530). The second follows from \(0.073>0.01\) and \(y>0\). Finally \(1+|\omega_1|^2|\wp_L|\le \max\{1,|\omega_1|^2\}(1+|\wp_L|)\), so the scaling identities prove (22.531). \(\square\)

The three bounds (22.515), (22.527) and (22.530) include the growth estimates of S. David, Minorations de formes linéaires de logarithmes elliptiques, Proposition 3.1. The product identities, constants and lattice scalings above give their proofs in the present normalization.

Periods, curve heights and explicit derivative bounds

We use the functions and lattice normalization of Propositions 22.175–22.183. Put \(Q=|q|=e^{-2\pi y}\), where \(q=e^{2\pi i\tau}\) and \(y=\operatorname{Im}\tau\ge\sqrt3/2\). In particular \(Q<1/230\). Decimal constants below are exact rational numbers. The algebraic curve convention in this section is \(Y^2=4X^3-g_2X-g_3\); its projective coordinates are \([1:\wp:\wp']\).

Proposition 22.184. Fourier expansions of the invariants

For \(r\ge1\), let \(\sigma_r(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^r\). Define

\[ E_4(q)=1+240\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_3(n)q^n, \qquad E_6(q)=1-504\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_5(n)q^n. \tag{22.533} \]

Then

\[ g_2(L_\tau)=\frac{4\pi^4}{3}E_4(q),\qquad g_3(L_\tau)=\frac{8\pi^6}{27}E_6(q), \qquad |g_2(L_\tau)|<272,\quad |g_3(L_\tau)|<1005. \tag{22.534} \]

Proof. In a small disc around zero, expand \(b/(1-b)^2=\sum_{m\ge1}mb^m\) in (22.497). Absolute convergence permits both summation and differentiation. Thus

\[ \wp_\tau(z)=\frac{\pi^2}{\sin^2(\pi z)}-\frac{\pi^2}{3} -4\pi^2\sum_{r,m\ge1}m q^{rm} (e^{2\pi imz}+e^{-2\pi imz}-2). \tag{22.535} \]

The first term minus its constant has expansion \(z^{-2}+\pi^4z^2/15+2\pi^6z^4/189+O(z^6)\), obtained by squaring and inverting the sine series. The coefficients of \(z^2\) and \(z^4\) in \(\wp\) are \(g_2/20\) and \(g_3/28\). Indeed, inserting \(\wp=z^{-2}+az^2+bz^4+O(z^6)\) in \(\wp'^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3\) gives \(20a=g_2\) and \(28b=g_3\) by comparing the coefficients of \(z^{-2}\) and one. Comparison in (22.535) gives (22.533)–(22.534), because \(\sum_{r,m\ge1}m^j q^{rm}=\sum_n\sigma_j(n)q^n\).

Applying \(Q\,d/dQ\) repeatedly to \(Q/(1-Q)\) gives

\[ \begin{split} \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n^3Q^n}{1-Q^n} &\le\frac{Q(1+4Q+Q^2)}{(1-Q)^5}=:S_3(Q),\\ \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n^5Q^n}{1-Q^n} &\le\frac{Q(1+26Q+66Q^2+26Q^3+Q^4)}{(1-Q)^7}=:S_5(Q). \end{split} \tag{22.536} \]

Here \((1-Q^n)^{-1}\le(1-Q)^{-1}\). The identities for \(\sum n^jQ^n\) follow inductively by differentiation, so no divisor-sum estimate has been omitted. Substituting \(Q=1/230\) and \(\pi<22/7\) gives the rational bounds

\[ \frac43(22/7)^4(1+240S_3(1/230))<272,\quad \frac8{27}(22/7)^6(1+504S_5(1/230))<1005. \tag{22.537} \]

All relevant series majorants increase with \(Q\), proving the assertions. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.185. A finite discriminant estimate

For \(0<|q|\le1/230\),

\[ \left|\frac{E_4(q)^3-E_6(q)^2}{1728q}-1\right|<\frac{11}{100}. \tag{22.538} \]

Consequently, with \(\Delta_\tau=g_2(L_\tau)^3-27g_3(L_\tau)^2\),

\[ \frac{89}{100}(2\pi)^{12}Q <|\Delta_\tau|<\frac{111}{100}(2\pi)^{12}Q. \tag{22.539} \]

Proof. We give a finite polynomial and tail calculation. The degree-four truncations of the two series are

\[ \begin{split} A(q)&=1+240q+2160q^2+6720q^3+17520q^4,\\ B(q)&=1-504q-16632q^2-122976q^3-532728q^4. \end{split} \tag{22.540} \]

For \(j>1\), \(\sigma_j(n)=n^j\sum_{d\mid n}d^{-j} \le n^j(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-j}\,dt) =j n^j/(j-1)\). The ratio of consecutive \(n^jQ^n\), for \(n\ge5\), is at most \((6/5)^jQ\). Therefore, for \(|q|\le Q\le1/230\),

\[ |E_4-A|\le R_4:=\frac{360\cdot5^3Q^5}{1-(6/5)^3Q}, \qquad |E_6-B|\le R_6:=\frac{630\cdot5^5Q^5}{1-(6/5)^5Q}. \tag{22.541} \]

Put \(A_+=1+240Q+2160Q^2+6720Q^3+17520Q^4\) and \(B_+=1+504Q+16632Q^2+122976Q^3+532728Q^4\). Let \(d_j=[q^j](A^3-B^2)\). Its coefficients for \(j=0,\ldots,12\) are, in that order,

\[ \begin{gathered} 0,\ 1728,\ -41472,\ 435456,\ -2543616,\ 5104512,\\ 1525813632,\ 50747641344,\ 424509633216,\\ 2050306560000,\ 4362564096000,\ 6188120064000,\ 5377771008000. \end{gathered} \tag{22.542} \]

It follows that the left side of (22.538) is at most

\[ \frac{\sum_{j=2}^{12}|d_j|Q^j +R_4(3A_+^2+3A_+R_4+R_4^2)+R_6(2B_++R_6)}{1728Q}. \tag{22.543} \]

Every summand after division by \(Q\) is increasing on this interval. Substitution of \(Q=1/230\) is a rational calculation and gives a value less than \(10924/100000<11/100\). Thus (22.538) follows. Finally \(\Delta_\tau=(64\pi^{12}/27)(E_4^3-E_6^2)\), and \((64/27)1728=4096=2^{12}\), giving (22.539). \(\square\)

Proposition 22.186. Period bounds and the imaginary part of the lattice

Let \(L=\omega_1(\mathbf Z+\tau\mathbf Z)\), \(g_2=g_2(L)\), \(g_3=g_3(L)\), and \(j=1728g_2^3/(g_2^3-27g_3^2)\). If \(j\ne0\), then

\[ \frac{e^{1.825-\pi y/6}|j|^{1/12}}{(12|g_2|)^{1/4}} \le |\omega_1|\le \frac{e^{1.85-\pi y/6}|j|^{1/12}}{(12|g_2|)^{1/4}}. \tag{22.544} \]

Suppose now that \(g_2,g_3\) belong to a number field of degree \(D\), at the given complex embedding, and put

\[ h_E=h(1:g_2:g_3),\qquad h=\max\{1,h_E,h(j)\}. \tag{22.545} \]

Then \(y\le Dh\), including when \(j=0\).

Proof. Lattice scaling gives \(g_2(L_\tau)=\omega_1^4g_2\) and \(g_3(L_\tau)=\omega_1^6g_3\), either from their lattice sums or their Laurent coefficients. Thus \(j\) is unchanged by scaling. If \(j\ne0\), then \(g_2\ne0\), and

\[ |\omega_1| =\frac{|\Delta_\tau|^{1/12}|j|^{1/12}} {(12|g_2|)^{1/4}}. \tag{22.546} \]

Apply (22.539). The elementary numerical comparisons required are \(2\pi(0.89)^{1/12}>e^{1.825}\) and \(2\pi(1.11)^{1/12}<e^{1.85}\). They follow using \(157/50<\pi<22/7\) from (22.503): the degree-twenty exponential sum with geometric remainder bounds \(e^{1.825}\) from above, and its degree-twenty sum bounds \(e^{1.85}\) from below. Raising the resulting positive rational inequalities to the twelfth power verifies both comparisons. This proves (22.544).

To control \(y\), there is nothing to prove if \(y\le1\). If \(y>1\), then \(Q<1/500\): the positive exponential sum \(\sum_{r=0}^{30}(157/25)^r/r!\) is greater than \(500\), and \(2\pi>157/25\). Equation (22.536) gives \(240S_3(1/500)<1/2\). Hence \(|E_4|>1/2\), and (22.538) gives

\[ |j|=\left|\frac{1728E_4^3}{E_4^3-E_6^2}\right| >\frac{25}{222Q}=\frac{25}{222}e^{2\pi y}>e^y. \tag{22.547} \]

For the last inequality, \((2\pi-1)y>5\) and \(e^5>1+5+25/2>222/25\). The chosen-embedding height bound \(\log\max\{1,|j|\}\le D h(j)\) now gives \(y<Dh\). This also shows that \(j=0\) forces \(y<1\), so no exceptional case has been omitted.

Every lattice admits the stipulated normalization. Choose a shortest nonzero vector \(\omega_1\). It is primitive in a lattice basis and therefore extends to a basis, by the integer Bézout identity. Choose the other vector's sign to make \(y>0\), and add an integer multiple of \(\omega_1\) so that \(|\operatorname{Re}\tau|\le1/2\). Minimality gives \(|\tau|\ge1\), whence \(y\ge\sqrt3/2\). \(\square\)

Theorem 22.187. Entire growth controlled by the curve height

For the curve and embedding of (22.545), the entire tuple \(\Phi_L\) of Theorem 22.179 satisfies

\[ \|\Phi_L(z)\|_\infty \le3.33\exp\left\{\frac34Dh_E +3\pi J_\tau(z/\omega_1)\right\}. \tag{22.548} \]

In particular this remains valid with \(J_\tau(w)\) replaced by \((\operatorname{Im}w)^2/y+|\operatorname{Im}w|+y/4\). The assertion includes curves with \(g_2=0\) or \(g_3=0\).

Proof. The separate bounds in (22.517) transform by the same scalar law as the tuple. They therefore give, for \(r=|\omega_1|\),

\[ \|\Phi_L(z)\|_\infty \le \max\{0.0176r^3,\ 0.309r,\ 3.33\} e^{3\pi J_\tau(z/\omega_1)}. \tag{22.549} \]

For a nonzero \(g_i\), the height definitions give \(\log\max\{1,|g_i|^{-1}\}\le D h_E\): projection bounds \(h(g_i)\) by \(h_E\), the product formula gives \(h(g_i^{-1})=h(g_i)\), and the nonnegative contribution of the chosen archimedean place is at least \(1/D\) times the relevant logarithm. These are the same height identities used in Lemma 22.141.

If \(g_2\ne0\), (22.534) implies \(r^4<272e^{Dh_E}\). Thus the first two factors in (22.549) are bounded by \(0.0176\,272^{3/4}e^{3Dh_E/4}\) and \(0.309\,272^{1/4}e^{Dh_E/4}\), respectively. Their constant factors are less than \(3.33\), as is checked by fourth powers. If \(g_2=0\), nonsingularity gives \(g_3\ne0\), and \(r^6<1005e^{Dh_E}\). The corresponding constants are \(0.0176\sqrt{1005}\) and \(0.309\,1005^{1/6}\), again less than \(3.33\); their height exponents are \(Dh_E/2\) and \(Dh_E/6\). Since \(h_E\ge0\), every case is bounded by (22.548). \(\square\)

Figure 22.14. Scaling the lattice by a complex number of modulus \(r\) multiplies the three coordinate bounds by \(r^3,r,1\). The solid black envelope in (22.549) retains these separate factors. The dashed curve is the coarser common factor \(3.33\max\{1,r^3\}\) from (22.516). Both are upper bounds; the curves do not plot values of an elliptic function.

Proposition 22.188. Explicit bounds for mixed directional derivatives

For \(i=1,\ldots,k\), let \(E_i\) and \(L_i=\omega_iL_{\tau_i}\) have the preceding normalization over a common field of degree \(D\). Put \(y_i=\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\) and \(h_i=h(1:g_{2,i}:g_{3,i})\). Let \(P\) be a polynomial of degree at most \(d_0\) in its additive variable and homogeneous degree \(d_i\) in the three coordinates of its \(i\)-th elliptic block. Suppose its \(N_P\ge1\) nonzero coefficients have modulus at most \(H_P\). Set

\[ F(z_0,\ldots,z_k)=P(z_0,\Phi_{L_1}(z_1),\ldots,\Phi_{L_k}(z_k)). \tag{22.550} \]

Choose directions \(x_1,\ldots,x_l\in\mathbf C^{k+1}\), nonnegative integers \(t_1,\ldots,t_l\), and write

\[ \begin{split} T&=\sum_at_a,\quad M_0=\min\{d_0,T\},\\ \xi_0&=\max\{1,|x_{a,0}|:1\le a\le l\},\\ \xi_1&=\max\{1,|x_{a,i}|:1\le a\le l,1\le i\le k\},\\ b_i&=|\operatorname{Im}(v_i/\omega_i)|+|\omega_i|^{-1}. \end{split} \tag{22.551} \]

With \(D_x=\sum_{i=0}^kx_i\partial/\partial z_i\),

\[ \begin{split} |D_{x_1}^{t_1}\cdots D_{x_l}^{t_l}F(v)| \le{}&N_PH_P\,T!(k+1)^T\xi_0^{M_0}\xi_1^T (|v_0|+1)^{d_0}\\ &\times\exp\left\{\sum_{i=1}^kd_i \left[\log(3.33)+\frac34Dh_i +3\pi\left(\frac{b_i^2}{y_i}+b_i+\frac{y_i}{4}\right)\right]\right\}. \end{split} \tag{22.552} \]

Here \(0!=1\); the estimate includes \(T=0\).

Proof. On the closed unit polydisc about \(v\), \(|z_0|\le|v_0|+1\), and \(|\operatorname{Im}(z_i/\omega_i)|\le b_i\). Bound each monomial by (22.548) and sum over the \(N_P\) coefficients. This gives the right side of (22.552) without its factor \(T!(k+1)^T\xi_0^{M_0}\xi_1^T\); denote that bound by \(M\). Iterating the one-variable Cauchy integral formula yields \(|\partial^\alpha F(v)|\le\alpha!M\) for \(|\alpha|=T\). This follows directly by integrating each variable on its unit circle, so the normalization of the derivatives is specified.

Expand the \(T\) directional derivative factors one at a time. There are \((k+1)^T\) terms before collecting equal partial derivatives. A surviving term chooses coordinate zero at most \(d_0\) times, since higher additive derivatives vanish. Its coefficient is at most \(\xi_0^{M_0}\xi_1^T\), and its partial derivative is at most \(T!M\), because \(\alpha!\le T!\). Summation proves (22.552). No estimate of \(N_P\) by an unspecified dimension is needed. \(\square\)

Exercise 22.189. The zero invariant case and height normalization

For \(E:Y^2=4X^3-1/2\), compute \(h_E\), \(h(j)\), and the exponents of \(r=|\omega_1|\) in its homogeneous lift. Give an explicit height-dependent upper bound for its tuple norm. Explain why a formula that divides by \(g_2\) cannot be used for this curve.

Solution. The primitive integral coordinates of \((1:0:1/2)\) are \((2:0:1)\), so \(h_E=\log2\). The invariant \(j\) is zero and has height zero. Scaling from \(L_\tau\) gives multipliers \(\omega_1^3,\omega_1,1\) on the three coordinates. Since \(g_3=1/2\), (22.534) gives \(r^6<2010\). Formula (22.549) therefore gives

\[ \|\Phi_L(z)\|_\infty \le\max\{0.0176\sqrt{2010},\ 0.309\,2010^{1/6},\ 3.33\} e^{3\pi J_\tau(z/\omega_1)} =3.33e^{3\pi J_\tau(z/\omega_1)}. \tag{22.553} \]

The equality of the constant to \(3.33\) is a finite positive-power comparison. The general height bound (22.548) also applies and gives the slightly larger prefactor \(3.33\,2^{3/4}\). Formula (22.544) does not apply: both \(j\) and \(g_2\) vanish, whereas the \(g_3\)-based argument above has a nonzero denominator. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.190. A uniform estimate near the pole

For \(0<|z|\le1/10\),

\[ |\wp_\tau(z)|\ge\frac{0.9}{|z|^2}. \tag{22.554} \]

Proof. The sine series and \(|z|\le1/10\) give

\[ |\sin(\pi z)|\le\pi|z|\, \frac{\sinh(\pi/10)}{\pi/10}<1.02\pi|z|. \tag{22.555} \]

For the last inequality, put \(u=11/35>\pi/10\). The series \(\sinh u/u\) is bounded by \(1+u^2/(6(1-u^2/20))<1.02\): after its quadratic term, successive ratios are at most \(u^2/20\).

Now \(|w|,|w|^{-1}\le e^{\pi/5}<15/8\). The last comparison follows from \(\pi/5<22/35\) and the degree-twenty exponential sum with geometric remainder. Isolating the trigonometric term in (22.497), its other terms have total modulus at most

\[ 4\pi^2\left\{\frac1{12} +\frac{(15/4)Q}{(1-Q)(1-15Q/8)^2} +\frac{2Q}{(1-Q)^3}\right\}<4.3. \tag{22.556} \]

Substitute \(Q=1/230\) and \(\pi=22/7\) to check the rational upper bound. Consequently \(|\wp_\tau(z)|\ge1/(1.02^2|z|^2)-4.3\). Since \(1/1.02^2-4.3/100>0.9\), (22.554) follows. \(\square\)

The period inequalities (22.544) are the estimates in S. David, Minorations de formes linéaires de logarithmes elliptiques, Lemma 3.2. The finite discriminant argument proves them here. Theorem 22.187 and Proposition 22.188 supply height-sensitive growth and derivative estimates with the support size of the polynomial explicitly retained.

Canonical heights from explicit duplication certificates

Let \(E/K\) be the nonsingular cubic

\[ E:\quad Y^2=4x^3-ax-b,\qquad \Delta=a^3-27b^2\ne0, \qquad h_E=h(1:a:b). \tag{22.557} \]

The absolute values and weights \(n_v/[K:\mathbf Q]\) are those of Lemma 22.47. For a finite point put \(h_x(P)=h(1:x(P))\) and \(h_3(P)=h(1:x(P):Y(P))\). Both heights are zero at \(O\). The subscript three records the plane embedding associated with \(3O\).

Proposition 22.191. The homogeneous duplication map

Define the binary quartics

\[ \begin{split} F(X,Z)&=16X^4+8aX^2Z^2+32bXZ^3+a^2Z^4,\\ G(X,Z)&=64X^3Z-16aXZ^3-16bZ^4. \end{split} \tag{22.558} \]

They have no common projective zero. If \(x(P)=[X:Z]\), with \(x(O)=[1:0]\), then \(x(2P)=[F(X,Z):G(X,Z)]\).

Proof. For \(Y(P)\ne0\), the tangent slope is \(m=(12x^2-a)/(2Y)\). The chord law on the cubic gives \(x(2P)=m^2/4-2x\), which is (22.558) after substituting \(Y^2=4x^3-ax-b\). To check that the formula extends everywhere, put \(f(x)=4x^3-ax-b\). Direct expansion gives

\[ F(x,1)=f'(x)^2-32xf(x),\qquad G(x,1)=16f(x). \tag{22.559} \]

A finite common zero would be a multiple root of \(f\), contrary to \(\Delta\ne0\). At \([1:0]\), \(F=16\) and \(G=0\). Thus the displayed pair defines a morphism on \(\mathbf P^1\). At a point with \(Y=0\) it gives infinity, as required for a point of order two; it fixes infinity. Equality on the remaining dense open set proves the duplication formula everywhere. \(\square\)

Lemma 22.192. Two polynomial identities with controlled coefficients

For a vector \(c=(c_0,\ldots,c_7)\), write

\[ A_c=\sum_{i=0}^3c_iX^{3-i}Z^i,\qquad B_c=\sum_{i=0}^3c_{i+4}X^{3-i}Z^i. \tag{22.560} \]

The two columns of the following table define vectors \(c,d\):

Index \(c_i\) \(d_i\)
0 \(256a^3-6912b^2\) \(0\)
1 \(-64a^2b\) \(-12288\)
2 \(-48a^4+1408ab^2\) \(0\)
3 \(-48a^3b+1536b^3\) \(4096a\)
4 \(16a^2b\) \(3072\)
5 \(-20a^4+512ab^2\) \(0\)
6 \(-104a^3b+3072b^3\) \(1280a\)
7 \(-3a^5+96a^2b^2\) \(6912b\)

Then

\[ A_cF+B_cG=4096\Delta X^7,\qquad A_dF+B_dG=4096\Delta Z^7. \tag{22.561} \]

Every coefficient polynomial in this table has total degree at most five. The sums of the absolute integer coefficients in the two columns are \(14095\) and \(27648\), respectively.

Proof. Multiply (22.558) by the degree-three polynomials in (22.560). In the first identity, the coefficient of \(X^7\) is \(16(256a^3-6912b^2)=4096\Delta\), and the coefficients of \(X^{7-i}Z^i\), \(1\le i\le7\), cancel. In the second, the only surviving coefficient is that of \(Z^7\), namely \(4096a\cdot a^2+6912b\cdot(-16b)=4096\Delta\). This proves the identities by coefficient comparison. The degrees and column sums follow directly from the table. \(\square\)

Proposition 22.193. Explicit errors in doubling the height

At an archimedean place, let

\[ U_v=\max\left\{\sum|\operatorname{coeff}(F)|_v, \sum|\operatorname{coeff}(G)|_v\right\}, \quad B_v=\max\left\{\sum_{i=0}^7|c_i|_v, \sum_{i=0}^7|d_i|_v\right\}. \tag{22.562} \]

At a nonarchimedean place replace each sum by a maximum. Define

\[ U_E=\sum_v\frac{n_v}{[K:\mathbf Q]}\log U_v, \qquad B_E=\sum_v\frac{n_v}{[K:\mathbf Q]}\log B_v. \tag{22.563} \]

These are nonnegative, finite, and unchanged by extending \(K\). For every \(P\in E(\overline{\mathbf Q})\),

\[ 4h_x(P)-B_E\le h_x(2P)\le4h_x(P)+U_E, \quad U_E\le2h_E+\log96,\quad B_E\le5h_E+\log27648. \tag{22.564} \]

Proof. Write \(N_v=\max\{|X|_v,|Z|_v\}\) and \(T_v=\max\{|F(X,Z)|_v,|G(X,Z)|_v\}\). The triangle or ultrametric inequality gives \(T_v\le U_vN_v^4\). Choose the identity (22.561) whose right side uses a coordinate of modulus \(N_v\). Its left side has modulus at most \(B_vN_v^3T_v\). Therefore

\[ \frac{|4096\Delta|_v}{B_v}N_v^4\le T_v\le U_vN_v^4. \tag{22.565} \]

Take weighted logarithms and sum. The product formula removes \(4096\Delta\), proving the height inequalities. This cancellation is why no inverse discriminant remains in the global error.

Set \(M_v=\max\{1,|a|_v,|b|_v\}\). At an archimedean place, \(U_v\le96M_v^2\) and \(B_v\le27648M_v^5\), by (22.558) and the table. At a finite place the corresponding bounds are \(M_v^2\) and \(M_v^5\), since the table has integer coefficients. The sum of archimedean weights is one. These facts give the last two assertions in (22.564).

Only finitely many finite places contribute to (22.563). Moreover \(U_v\ge|16|_v\) and \(B_v\ge|3072|_v\), so their global sums are nonnegative by the product formula. The local-degree identity under a field extension preserves the sums, exactly as in Lemma 22.47. Thus the inequalities hold for points over every finite extension and hence over \(\overline{\mathbf Q}\). \(\square\)

Theorem 22.194. Canonical height and a certified convergence interval

The limit

\[ \widehat h_x(P)=\lim_{r\to\infty}4^{-r}h_x(2^rP) \tag{22.566} \]

exists, is nonnegative, and satisfies

\[ h_x(P)-B_E/3\le\widehat h_x(P)\le h_x(P)+U_E/3, \qquad \widehat h_x(2P)=4\widehat h_x(P). \tag{22.567} \]

More generally, every integer \(r\ge0\) supplies the interval

\[ 4^{-r}h_x(2^rP)-\frac{B_E}{3\cdot4^r} \le\widehat h_x(P)\le 4^{-r}h_x(2^rP)+\frac{U_E}{3\cdot4^r}. \tag{22.568} \]

Proof. If \(a_r=4^{-r}h_x(2^rP)\), (22.564) gives \(-B_E4^{-r-1}\le a_{r+1}-a_r\le U_E4^{-r-1}\). The series of absolute differences converges, because its tail is bounded by a geometric series. Summing that tail from \(r\) to infinity gives (22.568). Nonnegativity follows from \(a_r\ge0\), and shifting the index in the limit gives the doubling law. The case \(r=0\) gives (22.567). \(\square\)

Proposition 22.195. Conversion to the plane height

For all \(P\in E(\overline{\mathbf Q})\),

\[ -\frac12h_E-\log2\le h_3(P)-\frac32h_x(P) \le\frac12h_E+\frac12\log6. \tag{22.569} \]

Consequently the canonical height for \(3O\) is

\[ \widehat h_3(P)=\lim_{r\to\infty}4^{-r}h_3(2^rP) =\frac32\widehat h_x(P), \tag{22.570} \]

and

\[ -C_-\le h_3(P)-\widehat h_3(P)\le C_+, \quad C_-=\frac12h_E+\log2+\frac12U_E, \quad C_+=\frac12h_E+\frac12\log6+\frac12B_E. \tag{22.571} \]

In particular,

\[ -\frac32h_E-\frac12\log384 \le h_3(P)-\widehat h_3(P) \le3h_E+\frac12\log165888. \tag{22.572} \]

Proof. At a finite point put \(u_v=\max\{1,|x|_v\}\), \(v_v=\max\{1,|x|_v,|Y|_v\}\), and use \(M_v\) from Proposition 22.193. The curve equation gives \(v_v\le\sqrt6\,M_v^{1/2}u_v^{3/2}\) at an archimedean place and \(v_v\le M_v^{1/2}u_v^{3/2}\) at a finite place. Indeed, the three terms \(4x^3,-ax,-b\) have total absolute value at most \(6M_vu_v^3\) in the first case and maximum at most \(M_vu_v^3\) in the second. Also \(u_v\le u_v^{3/2}\).

For the opposite inequality there is nothing to prove if \(u_v=1\). Otherwise write \(4x^3=Y^2+ax+b\). At an archimedean place, \(4u_v^3\le3M_vv_v^2\), and hence \(u_v^3\le M_vv_v^2\). At a finite place, \(u_v^3\le |4|_v^{-1}M_vv_v^2\). The same inequalities hold when \(u_v=1\), since \(M_v,v_v\ge1\) and \(|4|_v\le1\) at finite places. The sum of the finite-place contributions \(-\log|4|_v\) is \(\log4\), by the product formula. Weighted logarithms of these upper and lower estimates prove (22.569), including the contribution at primes above two. At \(O\) both point heights vanish, so the assertion still holds.

Apply (22.569) to \(2^rP\) and divide by \(4^r\); its error tends to zero, proving (22.570). Combining (22.569) with (22.567) gives (22.571). Substitution of the last two bounds in (22.564) gives (22.572), since \(4\cdot96=384\) and \(6\cdot27648=165888\). \(\square\)

Corollary 22.196. Quadratic heights of arbitrary multiples

For every integer \(n\),

\[ \widehat h_3(nP)=n^2\widehat h_3(P),\qquad n^2\widehat h_3(P)-C_- \le h_3(nP)\le n^2\widehat h_3(P)+C_+. \tag{22.573} \]

In particular \(\widehat h_3(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-2}h_3(nP)\). If \(V\ge\max\{1,h_E,\widehat h_3(P)\}\), then

\[ h_3(nP)\le(n^2+10)V\qquad(n\in\mathbf Z). \tag{22.574} \]

Proof. The morphism \(x:E\to\mathbf P^1\) has pole divisor \(2O\); its local pole has order two, as in the Weierstrass uniformization. Thus \(h_x\) is a height of the symmetric line bundle \(\mathcal O_E(2O)\). The identity \([n]^*M\simeq M^{\otimes n^2}\) for a symmetric line bundle is proved in Abelian varieties, Theorem 5.1. The height identities proved in Proposition 22.49 therefore give, for each fixed \(n\), a bound \(|h_x(nQ)-n^2h_x(Q)|\le A_n\) independent of \(Q\). Use \(Q=2^rP\), divide by \(4^r\), and let \(r\to\infty\). Commutation of multiplication maps proves the scaling law for \(\widehat h_x\), and (22.570) proves it for \(\widehat h_3\). The case \(n=0\) follows from \(h_x(O)=0\); negative \(n\) also follow from \(x(-P)=x(P)\). Now apply (22.571) to \(nP\). Dividing its uniform error by \(n^2\) proves the stated limit.

Finally \(\tfrac12\log165888<7\): the positive exponential sum \(\sum_{r=0}^{20}14^r/r!\) already exceeds \(165888\). Thus (22.572) gives \(C_+\le3h_E+\tfrac12\log165888<10V\), proving (22.574). The constant \(A_n\) was used only to identify the exact scaling law; it does not occur in either explicit bound. \(\square\)

Exercise 22.197. A rational point with certified positive height

Let \(E:Y^2=4x^3-8\) and \(P=(3,10)\). Compute \(U_E,B_E\) from (22.562)–(22.563), compute \(2P\), and use one doubling to prove that \(P\) is nontorsion.

Solution. For integral coefficients, the finite-place contribution to \(U_E\) is minus the logarithm of the gcd of all coefficients of \(F,G\). For \(B_E\) it is minus the logarithm of the gcd of all entries of the two columns in Lemma 22.192. This follows prime by prime from the maximum in the nonarchimedean norm. Here the respective archimedean maxima and gcds are

\[ U_\infty=272,\quad \gcd(\operatorname{coeff}F, \operatorname{coeff}G)=16,\qquad B_\infty=2801664,\quad \gcd(c_0,\ldots,d_7)=3072. \tag{22.575} \]

Hence \(U_E=\log17\), \(B_E=\log912\), and \(h_E=\log8\). The tangent slope is \(27/5\), so \(2P=(129/100,-383/500)\). These coordinates satisfy the curve equation. Their plane height is \(\log645\), while \(h_x(2P)=\log129\). From (22.568) and (22.570),

\[ \frac18\log\frac{129^3}{912} \le\widehat h_3(P)\le\frac18\log(129^3\cdot17). \tag{22.576} \]

The left endpoint is positive because \(129^3>912\). A torsion point has canonical height zero by (22.573), so \(P\) is nontorsion.

For additional precision, reduce the integer pair

\[ (N,D)\longmapsto (N^4+16ND^3,\ 4N^3D-8D^4) \tag{22.577} \]

by its gcd after each step, starting from \((3,1)\). If \(H_r=\max\{|N_r|,|D_r|\}\), the exact interval is

\[ \frac{3\log H_r-\log912}{2\cdot4^r} \le\widehat h_3(P)\le \frac{3\log H_r+\log17}{2\cdot4^r}. \tag{22.578} \]

Its width is \(\log(912\cdot17)/(2\cdot4^r)\). Every endpoint is determined by integer arithmetic and a logarithm; the validity of the interval follows from the proved tail bound. \(\square\)

Figure 22.15. The intervals in (22.578) for successive doublings of \((3,10)\) on \(Y^2=4x^3-8\). The endpoints are displayed numerically; their defining integer recurrence and logarithmic expressions are exact. The width decreases by a factor of four at every step.

Canonical versus projective height estimates are used in S. David, Minorations de formes linéaires de logarithmes elliptiques, Lemma 3.4. The estimates (22.571)–(22.572) use the explicit duplication certificates displayed here and the plane-height normalization specified in (22.557).

A uniform arithmetic estimate for the first elliptic jet

Let \(E:y^2=x^3+Ax+B\) be nonsingular over a number field. Use plane coordinates \([X:Y:Z]\), with identity \([0:1:0]\). Write \(Q=[u:v:w]\) for a second point, so \(v^2w=u^3+Auw^2+Bw^3\). All logarithmic heights use the absolute normalization of Lemma 22.47.

Lemma 22.198. An explicit translation tuple at the identity

Define the following polynomials of bidegree \((2,2)\):

\[ \begin{split} T_X={}&-Au^2Z^2+Aw^2X^2-3BuwZ^2+3Bw^2XZ\\ &+2uvYZ+uwY^2-v^2XZ-2vwXY,\\ T_Y={}&AuvZ^2-2AuwYZ+2AvwXZ-Aw^2XY\\ &+3BvwZ^2-3Bw^2YZ-3u^2XY+3uvX^2-v^2YZ+vwY^2,\\ T_Z={}&AuwZ^2-Aw^2XZ+3u^2XZ-3uwX^2-v^2Z^2+w^2Y^2. \end{split} \tag{22.579} \]

Where this tuple is nonzero it represents addition of the two points. For every finite \(Q\), it is nonzero at the first identity, and

\[ T((0,1,0),Q)=wQ. \tag{22.580} \]

At an archimedean place the sum of the absolute coefficients of each coordinate polynomial is at most \(20\max(1,|A|,|B|)\). At a finite place its maximum coefficient modulus is at most \(\max(1,|A|,|B|)\).

Proof. On the affine open \(Z=w=1\), put \(d=x-u\) and \(N_x=(y-v)^2-(x+u)d^2\). Reduction by the two curve equations gives the three polynomial identities

\[ T_Z=d^3,\qquad T_X=dN_x,\qquad T_Y=-yd^3+(y-v)(xd^2-N_x). \tag{22.581} \]

For example, replace \(x^3\) by \(y^2-Ax-B\) and \(u^3\) by \(v^2-Au-B\), and expand. The resulting expressions are exactly (22.579) with \(Z=w=1\). When \(d\ne0\), the ratios are the chord formulas \(x(P+Q)=N_x/d^2\) and \(y(P+Q)=-y+(y-v)(x-N_x/d^2)/d\). Homogenization and equality of projective cross products extend this identity wherever the tuple is nonzero. Substitution of \((X,Y,Z)=(0,1,0)\) gives (22.580); a finite point has \(w\ne0\).

The three coefficient sums are bounded respectively by \(2|A|+6|B|+6\), \(6|A|+6|B|+8\), and \(2|A|+8\). Each is at most the asserted archimedean bound. All coefficients are integers times \(1,A,B\); integers have finite-place modulus at most one. This proves the other bound. At \(Q=O\), translation is instead represented by the identity tuple \((X,Y,Z)\). Thus the displayed law supplies a frame near the first identity for every translation. It is not asserted to be nonzero at every pair of points. \(\square\)

Proposition 22.199. A formal coefficient bound with specified constants

For \(1\le i\le g\), let \(E_i:y^2=x^3+A_ix+B_i\) and \(q_i\in E_i(L)\), where \(L\) is a number field of degree \(e\). Put

\[ H_i=h(1:A_i:B_i),\qquad \mu_E=\sum_v w_v\log\max_i(1,|A_i|_v^{1/4},|B_i|_v^{1/6}), \qquad \mu_E\le\frac14\sum_iH_i. \tag{22.582} \]

Here \(w_v=[L_v:\mathbf Q_v]/e\). Normalize a representative \(Q_i\) of each finite \(q_i\) to have one coordinate equal to one. Let \(V_i(t)=(-t,1,-s_i(t))\), as in Lemma 22.163, and set \(G_i(t)=T_i(V_i(t),Q_i)\). If \(q_i=O\), set \(G_i=V_i\).

Let \(P\) have multidegree \((d,D_1,\ldots,D_g)\), with nonnegative integer degrees and \(N_P\ge1\) nonzero coefficients. For \(a,\beta_i\in L\), put

\[ \mathscr H(t)=P\left(1,a+\sum_i\beta_i\ell_i(t_i), G_1(t_1),\ldots,G_g(t_g)\right), \qquad H_{a,\beta}=h(1:a:\beta_1:\cdots:\beta_g). \tag{22.583} \]

For \(|\nu|=N\), its coefficient \(c_\nu=[t^\nu]\mathscr H\) satisfies

\[ \begin{split} h(c_\nu)\le\mathcal B_N:={}&h_c(P)+\log N_P +d\{H_{a,\beta}+\log(g+1)\}\\ &+\sum_iD_i\{2h(q_i)+H_i+\log20\}\\ &+N(\log8+\mu_E)+\log\Delta_N(d). \end{split} \tag{22.584} \]

The denominator \(\Delta_N(d)\) is defined in Lemma 22.137. If \(c_\nu\ne0\), then \(\log|c_\nu|\ge-e\mathcal B_N\) at any specified complex embedding.

Proof. Put \(M_{i,v}=\max(1,|A_i|_v,|B_i|_v)\), \(q_{i,v}=\max_j|Q_{i,j}|_v\), and let \(M_v\) be the maximum inside (22.582). At a finite place, Lemmas 22.163 and 22.198 give

\[ |[t^m]G_{i,j}|_v\le M_{i,v}q_{i,v}^2M_v^m. \tag{22.585} \]

For \(q_i=O\), take \(q_{i,v}=1\); the same bound follows directly from \(G_i=V_i\). At an infinite place, the series norm at radius \((8M_v)^{-1}\) is at most \(20M_{i,v}q_{i,v}^2\), by the coefficient sum in Lemma 22.198. The coefficient argument in Proposition 22.164 now applies: an additive monomial uses at most \(d\) logarithm factors, whose denominators divide \(\Delta_N(d)\), and its \(a,\beta\) degree is at most \(d\). At infinity its series norm is bounded by \(((g+1)\max(1,|a|_v,|\beta|_v))^d\). The \(N_P\) monomials contribute the factor \(N_P\) at infinity. Taking weighted logarithms yields exactly (22.584).

The inequality for \(\mu_E\) follows place by place from \(M_v\le\prod_iM_{i,v}^{1/4}\). All constants are nonnegative and unchanged by a field extension. The product-formula lower bound of Lemma 22.47 proves the assertion about a nonzero coefficient. This proof includes \(N=0\), \(d=0\), and identity translations; in the first two cases \(\Delta_N(d)=1\). \(\square\)

Lemma 22.200. A lower bound for the entire lift at every logarithm

Put \(a=-4A\), \(b=-4B\), and

\[ h_E=h(1:a:b),\qquad h_* =\max\{1,h_E,h(j(E))\}. \tag{22.586} \]

Let \(L_E=\omega_1(\mathbf Z+\tau\mathbf Z)\) be a reduced period lattice for the differential \(dx/(2y)\). Use the entire tuple \(\Phi_{L_E}\) of Theorem 22.179, in its coordinate order \((\phi^3,\phi^3\wp,\phi^3\wp')\). The tuple

\[ \Psi_E(z)=\bigl(\Phi_{L_E,1}(z), \tfrac12\Phi_{L_E,2}(z), \Phi_{L_E,0}(z)\bigr) \tag{22.587} \]

represents \([x(z):y(z):1]\), and for every \(z\in\mathbf C\),

\[ \|\Psi_E(z)\|_\infty\ge \exp(-21eh_*). \tag{22.588} \]

Proof. Write \(y_\tau=\operatorname{Im}\tau\). Proposition 22.186 gives \(y_\tau\le eh_*\). The discriminant estimate of Proposition 22.185 and lattice scaling give

\[ |\omega_1|^{12}|a^3-27b^2| \ge0.89(2\pi)^{12}e^{-2\pi y_\tau},\qquad |a^3-27b^2|\le28e^{3eh_E}. \tag{22.589} \]

The constant \(0.89(2\pi)^{12}/28\) exceeds one, since \(2\pi>6\). Therefore \(\log|\omega_1|\ge-(\pi/6+1/4)eh_*>-eh_*\). This argument includes \(a=0\) and \(b=0\); the discriminant itself is nonzero.

In (22.528), \(J_\tau(w)=(\operatorname{Im}w-y_\tau/2)^2/y_\tau\ge0\). The coordinate permutation and the factor \(1/2\) in (22.587) thus give

\[ \|\Psi_E(z)\|_\infty \ge\frac{0.073^3}{2} \exp\{-(3+3\pi)eh_*\}. \tag{22.590} \]

Finally \(\log(2/0.073^3)<60/7\): the rational sum \(\sum_{r=0}^{30}(60/7)^r/r!\) exceeds \(2/0.073^3\). Together with \(\pi<22/7\), this implies \(3+3\pi+\log(2/0.073^3)<21\). Since \(eh_*\ge1\), (22.590) proves (22.588). The argument is uniform in \(z\), including lattice points and every choice of logarithm branch. \(\square\)

Theorem 22.201. A completely specified first-jet lower bound

For the curves and polynomial of Proposition 22.199, write \(h_{*,i}\) for (22.586). Choose logarithms \(v_i\) of \(q_i\) and use the lifts \(\Psi_i\) from (22.587). Define

\[ F_q(z)=P\left(1,a+\sum_i\beta_i z_i, \Psi_1(v_1+z_1),\ldots,\Psi_g(v_g+z_g)\right). \tag{22.591} \]

If its first nonzero total degree is \(N\), every nonzero degree-\(N\) coefficient \(f_\nu\) satisfies

\[ \log|f_\nu|\ge -e\left(\mathcal B_N+21\sum_iD_i h_{*,i}\right). \tag{22.592} \]

In particular, let \(p_i\in E_i(L)\) have logarithms \(u_i\), let \(a=su_0\), \(q_i=[s]p_i\), \(v_i=su_i\), and let \(s\in\mathbf Z\). Write \(H=h(1:u_0:\beta_1:\cdots:\beta_g)\) and choose real numbers \(\mathcal V_i\ge\max\{h_{*,i},\widehat h_3(p_i)\}\), where \(\widehat h_3\) has the normalization of (22.570). Then

\[ \begin{split} \log|f_\nu|\ge-e\bigg[&h_c(P)+\log N_P +d\{H+\log((g+1)\max(1,|s|))\}\\ &+\sum_iD_i(2s^2+48)\mathcal V_i\\ &+N\left\{\log8+\frac14\sum_i(\mathcal V_i+\log4) +2(\log2)H_{\min(d,N)}\right\}\bigg]. \end{split} \tag{22.593} \]

Here \(H_m=\sum_{r=1}^m1/r\) and \(H_0=0\).

Proof. Normalize \(Q_i\) at a coordinate where \(\Psi_i(v_i)\) has largest modulus. Thus all coordinates of \(Q_i\) have modulus at most one at the chosen embedding, and \(\Psi_i(v_i)=\kappa_iQ_i\), with \(|\kappa_i|=\|\Psi_i(v_i)\|_\infty\). For finite \(q_i\), Lemma 22.198 gives \(G_i(0)=b_iQ_i\), where \(b_i=Q_{i,Z}\ne0\) and \(|b_i|\le1\). At \(q_i=O\), take \(Q_i=(0,1,0)\) and \(b_i=1\).

The first homogeneous part is unchanged by \(z_i=\ell_i(t_i)=t_i+O(t_i^2)\), as proved in Proposition 22.138. The two local lifts differ by holomorphic units, so the same first-degree comparison as (22.462) gives

\[ f_\nu=c_\nu\prod_i(\kappa_i/b_i)^{D_i},\qquad c_\nu\ne0. \tag{22.594} \]

Use Proposition 22.199, \(|b_i|\le1\), and (22.588) to prove (22.592). No estimate for the inverse translation scalar is needed.

For the sampled assertion, multiplication of one homogeneous coordinate by \(s\) gives \(H_{su_0,\beta}\le H+\log\max(1,|s|)\), also for \(s=0\). Changing from \([1:x:2y]\) to \([x:y:1]\) changes height by at most \(\log2\). Corollary 22.196 therefore gives \(h(q_i)\le(s^2+10)\mathcal V_i+\log2\). Also \(H_i\le h_{E_i}+\log4\le\mathcal V_i+\log4\). Consequently

\[ 2h(q_i)+H_i+\log20+21h_{*,i} \le(2s^2+42)\mathcal V_i+\log320 <(2s^2+48)\mathcal V_i. \tag{22.595} \]

Here \(\log320<6\), as follows already by summing \(\sum_{r=0}^{12}6^r/r!>320\). Finally use (22.582) and \(\log\Delta_N(d)\le2(\log2)N H_{\min(d,N)}\) from Lemma 22.137. This proves (22.593), including zero coordinates, torsion samples, negative \(s\), \(d=0\), and \(N=0\). \(\square\)

Exercise 22.202. Translation by a point of order two

On \(E:y^2=x^3-x\), let \(q=(0,0)\). Find the tuple (22.579) for translation by \(q\), prove that its square represents the identity wherever defined, and compute its first jet at \(O\).

Solution. Substitution gives

\[ T_q(X,Y,Z)=(-X^2,XY,Y^2+XZ),\qquad T_q(T_q(X,Y,Z))=-X^3(X,Y,Z). \tag{22.596} \]

The second identity is a direct polynomial identity in three independent variables. Thus the translation is an involution on a dense open set, hence on the curve; \(q\ne O\) has order two. The tuple is nonzero at \(O\), where it equals \((0,0,1)\).

Here \(s=t^3-ts^2=t^3-t^7+O(t^{11})\), so evaluation at \(V(t)=(-t,1,-s(t))\) gives

\[ (x_q(t),y_q(t))= \left(\frac{-t^2}{1+ts(t)},\frac{-t}{1+ts(t)}\right), \qquad (x_q'(0),y_q'(0))=(0,-1). \tag{22.597} \]

This agrees with the invariant vector field \((2y,3x^2-1)\) at \((0,0)\), since \(\ell'(0)=1\). In particular the \(y\)-coordinate has first coefficient \(-1\). The local scalar is one even though \(q\) is a point with zero \(y\)-coordinate. For \(P=Y\), (22.584) gives the explicit upper bound \(\log160\) for the height of this coefficient; its actual height is zero. \(\square\)

Figure 22.16. The map in (22.597) sends a neighborhood of the identity, parametrized by \(t\), to the branch through \((0,0)\). The left panel shows its image and the tangent direction for increasing \(t\). The two right panels show the coordinate functions and their first terms \(-t^2\) and \(-t\). The algebraic formula and the derivative are exact; plotted points are numerical evaluations of the formal branch.

The first-jet method is discussed in É. Gaudron, Mesures d'indépendance linéaire de logarithmes dans un groupe algébrique commutatif, Sections 6.11–6.13. The entire-coordinate bounds used here are proved in Theorems 22.179 and 22.182, with comparison to S. David, Minorations de formes linéaires de logarithmes elliptiques, Proposition 3.1. All constants in (22.593) are specified by the displayed curve, polynomial and height data.

Numerical weights and a stronger multiplicity estimate

Let \(g\ge1\), \(n=g+1\), and let \(E_i\) and \(p_i\in E_i(K)\) be elliptic curves and points over a number field \(K\) of degree \(D\), in the models of (22.557) and (22.586). Choose nonzero complex logarithms \(u_i\) of \(p_i\). Put \(h=\max_i h_{*,i}\). Choose real height budgets \(v_i\) and parameters \(B,E\) satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} b=\log B\ge \mathrm e h,\qquad Db\ge v_1\ge\cdots\ge v_g\ge h,\qquad v_i\ge\widehat h_3(p_i),\qquad \ell=\log E\ge1,\\ E\le\frac{\mathrm e\sqrt{Dv_i}\,|\omega_{1,i}| \sqrt{\operatorname{Im}\tau_i}} {\sqrt{3\pi}\,|u_i|}\quad(1\le i\le g). \end{gathered} \tag{22.598} \]

The requirement \(u_i\ne0\) makes each denominator meaningful. Terms with zero logarithm can be omitted before choosing these parameters. Throughout this section \(\mathrm e=\exp(1)\).

Lemma 22.203. A height bound for the analytic parameter

Under (22.598),

\[ \ell\le5Dv_g,\qquad L=\log b+h+\log D+\ell\le R=b+\log D+\ell,\qquad L\ge\ell. \tag{22.599} \]

Proof. Fix one index, write \(H=Dv_i\ge1\), \(y=\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\), \(\omega=\omega_{1,i}\), and \(r=|u_i/\omega|>0\). Proposition 22.186 gives \(y\le H\). If \(r\ge1/10\), (22.598) gives \(\ell\le1+\log H+\log(10/3)<3H\), since \(\pi>3\), \(\log H\le H-1\), and \(\log(10/3)<2\).

Suppose \(r<1/10\). A nonzero point of a reduced normalized lattice has modulus at least one, by the shortest-vector construction in Proposition 22.186. Thus \(p_i\ne O\). Proposition 22.190 gives \(|u_i|^2\ge0.9/|x(p_i)|\). The canonical-height bound (22.567) implies

\[ h_x(p_i)\le\tfrac23\widehat h_3(p_i) +\tfrac53h_{E_i}+\tfrac13\log27648\le6v_i. \tag{22.600} \]

Here \(\log27648<11\), as is certified by the positive sum \(\sum_{j=0}^{25}11^j/j!>27648\).

We also have \(\log(|\omega|\sqrt y/\sqrt{3\pi})\le H/3\). For a nonzero invariant \(a_i\), (22.544) gives \(\log|\omega|\le1.85-\tfrac14\log12-\pi y/6+H/3\). The maximum of \(\tfrac12\log y-\pi y/6\) is \(\tfrac12\log(3/\pi)-1/2\), by differentiation. The remaining constant is \(1.35-\tfrac14\log12-\log\pi<0\): use \(\pi>3\), \(\mathrm e<3\), and \(9<12\). If \(a_i=0\), then \(j(E_i)=0\), hence \(y\le1\) by Proposition 22.186. The bound \(|g_3(\tau_i)|<1005\) gives \(\log|\omega|\le(\log1005+H)/6\). Since \(1005<2\cdot729<\mathrm e(3\pi)^3\), the same assertion follows from \(H\ge1\).

The height bound for a complex coordinate now yields

\[ \ell\le1+\tfrac12\log H+\tfrac D2h_x(p_i) +H/3+\tfrac12\log(10/9)<\tfrac92H<5H. \tag{22.601} \]

Indeed \(1+\tfrac12\log H\le H\) and \(\tfrac12\log(10/9)<1/6\), because \(\exp(1/3)>1+1/3>10/9\). Apply the result to every index. Finally \(b\ge\mathrm e\) gives \(\log b\le b/\mathrm e\), by maximizing \(\log t/t\). Also \(h\le b/\mathrm e\). Thus \(\log b+h\le2b/\mathrm e<b\), proving the last claims of (22.599). \(\square\)

Lemma 22.204. Explicit preliminary degrees

Define positive constants, depending only on \(g\), by

\[ \begin{gathered} \epsilon=\frac1{200g^2},\quad \lambda=2\epsilon,\quad A_g=g\log(4n)+5\log n+15,\\ J_g=\frac{12(13+4\mathrm e^2)}{25+4\mathrm e^2} n\log(4n)+56\log n+54,\\ c_4=4^g n^{g+1}(1+\lambda)8n A_gJ_g,\qquad c_6=n2^g,\\ c_7=\frac{4\log(4n)}{13+4\mathrm e^2} +\frac{60+20\log n}{(13+4\mathrm e^2)g},\qquad c_5=\frac{c_6c_4^{2g+1}}{n!6^gc_7^g}. \end{gathered} \tag{22.602} \]

Set

\[ \begin{gathered} S=\left\lfloor\frac{c_4DL}{\ell}\right\rfloor,\qquad U_0=c_5D^{2g+2}RL^{g+1}\left(\prod_i v_i\right)\ell^{-2g-1},\\ \Theta=\frac{U_0}{DL},\qquad t_i=\frac{c_7U_0}{DS^2v_i}\quad(1\le i\le g),\qquad C=(1+\epsilon)2^g. \end{gathered} \tag{22.603} \]

These numbers satisfy

\[ \begin{gathered} \frac{c_4DL}{2\ell}\le S\le\frac{c_4DL}{\ell},\qquad \Theta>800g^3n,\quad \Theta\ge c_4,\quad t_i>400g^3+1,\\ M:=\min_i\frac{\Theta}{t_i} =\frac{S^2v_g}{c_7L}\ge\frac{c_4^2}{20c_7}>6n. \end{gathered} \tag{22.604} \]

Proof. The elementary estimates

\[ c_4\ge6480\,4^gn^{g+2},\qquad c_4>10^5n^2, \qquad 0<c_7<5n \tag{22.605} \]

are useful. The first uses \(A_g>15\), \(J_g>54\). For the second, \(\log2>3/5\) follows from \(\mathrm e<3\) and \(3^3<2^5\). Hence \(A_g>19\), \(J_g>85\), and \(4^gn^g\ge8\), giving \(c_4>103360n^2\). For the last use \(\log(4n)\le2n\), \(\log n\le n\), and \(n\ge2\): the numerator defining \(c_7\), with \(1/g\le1\), is at most \(28n+60\le58n\), while its denominator exceeds 13.

Since \(DL/\ell\ge1\), taking the floor loses at most half. Moreover (22.599) gives \(v_i\ge\ell/(5D)\). Substitution into (22.603), using \(R,L\ge\ell\), gives

\[ \Theta\ge c_5/5^g,\qquad t_i\ge\frac{c_7c_5}{5^{g-1}c_4^2}. \tag{22.606} \]

Using \(n!\le n^n\), \(c_7<5n\), and \(c_6\ge1\), the first bound is greater than \(10^5n^{2g+1}\), and its ratio to \(c_4\) is at least \(c_4^{2g}/(150^gn^{2g+1})>1\). Since \(n^{2g}\ge g^3\), this proves both assertions about \(\Theta\). The second bound is at least

\[ \frac{c_4^{2g-1}}{150^gn^{2g}} >\frac{2000}{3}\left(\frac{10^{10}}{150}\right)^{g-1} n^{2g-2}\ge\frac{2000}{3}g^3>400g^3+1. \tag{22.607} \]

For \(g=1,2\), the penultimate comparison is direct; for \(g\ge3\), use \(2g-2\ge3\) and \(n\ge g\). Finally the lower bound for \(S\), followed by \(v_g\ge\ell/(5D)\) and \(L\ge\ell\), proves the bound for \(M\). In fact (22.605) gives \(c_4^2/(20c_7)>10^8n^3>6n\). \(\square\)

Proposition 22.205. An extremal additive degree

Let \(p\in G=\mathbf G_a\times\prod_iE_i\), and let \(W=\{z_0=\sum_i\beta_i z_i\}\), with every \(\beta_i\ne0\). For each connected subgroup \(H=\{0\}\times B\) whose Lie algebra is contained in \(W\), put \(h_B=\dim B\), \(q_B=g-h_B\), and \(Q_B=\#\{sp+H:0\le s<S\}\). Write \(P_q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^q(z+j)\), and define

\[ t_0=\min_B \frac{P_{q_B}(\Theta)Q_B\mathcal H_B(t_1,\ldots,t_g)} {C n!3^g\prod_i t_i}. \tag{22.608} \]

The minimum exists, is attained, and satisfies

\[ 400g^3+1<t_0\le\frac{U_0}{c_6DR},\qquad P_{q_B}(\Theta)Q_B\mathcal H_B(t)\ge C\mathcal H_G(t) \tag{22.609} \]

for every such \(B\), with equality for a minimizing \(B_*\). Every integer \(L_i=\lfloor t_i\rfloor\), including \(i=0\), is greater than \(400g^3\).

Proof. The multidegree polynomials in Proposition 22.149 have nonnegative integer coefficients and a positive coefficient. At fixed positive weights, a bounded value bounds each of those integers. The dimension has finitely many possibilities and \(1\le Q_B\le S\). Hence the same finite-coefficient argument as in Lemma 22.151 gives a positive attained minimum.

For the point subgroup, \(\mathcal H_{\{0\}}=1\) and \(Q_{\{0\}}\le S\). Direct substitution of (22.602)–(22.603) shows that its value divided by \(U_0/(c_6DR)\) is at most

\[ \frac1{1+\epsilon}\prod_{j=1}^g(1+j/\Theta)\le1. \tag{22.610} \]

Indeed \(\sum j/\Theta<\epsilon/8\), by (22.604), and \(\prod(1+x_j)\le\exp(\sum x_j)\le1+\epsilon/4\). The last step follows from \(e^x\le(1-x)^{-1}\le1+2x\) for \(0\le x\le1/2\). This proves the upper bound.

At a minimizing subgroup of dimension \(h_B\), set \(q=g-h_B\ge1\). A positive monomial of \(\mathcal H_B\) has coefficient at least \(h_B!3^{h_B}\). Equality in (22.609) and \(P_q(\Theta)\ge\Theta^q\) give

\[ t_0\ge\frac{h_B!}{Cn!} \left(\frac{c_4^2}{60c_7}\right)^q. \tag{22.611} \]

Put \(A=c_4^2/(60c_7)\). There are \(q+1\) factors in \(n!/h_B!\), each at most \(n\), and \(A>n\). Thus the right side is at least \(A/(Cn^2)\). From (22.605) and \(C<2^{g+1}\), this exceeds \(69984\,8^gn^{2g+1}>400g^3+1\). The remaining assertions follow from the definition of the minimum and (22.604). \(\square\)

Lemma 22.206. Counting powers of an ideal

Let \(R\) be a regular local ring of dimension \(r\), containing a characteristic-zero field. Let \(I\) be primary for its maximal ideal. Suppose \(\rho\) transverse derivations, normalized as in (22.61), send every element of \(I\) into the maximal ideal after every word of length at most \(T\). Assume that these derivations extend to a set of \(r\) derivations dual modulo the maximal ideal to a regular parameter system. If a parameter ideal \(J\subset I\) is generated by a regular sequence, then

\[ \operatorname{length}(R/J)\ge(T+1)^\rho. \tag{22.612} \]

The assertion includes \(\rho=0\).

Proof. Put \(a=T+1\). For a word applied to a product of \(m\) elements of \(I\), call the first \(\rho\) derivations the selected ones. If it has \(b\) other derivations and fewer than \(a(m-b)\) selected derivations, one of the \(m\) factors receives no other derivation and at most \(T\) selected ones. Every term of the product rule therefore vanishes in the residue field. This applies to every element of \(I^m\).

Use the filtration and coefficient-lifting proof of Theorem 22.25, now with all \(r\) parameters. In each ordinary degree it proves independence, modulo \(I^m\) and the next maximal-ideal power, of the monomials \(z^\alpha\) satisfying

\[ |\alpha_{1:\rho}|<a\bigl(m-|\alpha_{\rho+1:r}|\bigr). \tag{22.613} \]

For each selected multiindex, use the word with those exact derivation counts. The normalized linear action kills every other monomial of the same total degree, just as in (22.64). Consequently \(\operatorname{length}(R/I^m)\) is at least the number \(N_m\) of these monomials.

If \(0<\rho<r\), this count is

\[ N_m=\sum_{b=0}^{m-1} \binom{b+r-\rho-1}{r-\rho-1} \binom{a(m-b)+\rho-1}{\rho},\qquad \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{r!N_m}{m^r}=a^\rho. \tag{22.614} \]

To obtain the limit, use the leading terms of the two binomial polynomials and the Riemann sum on \([0,1]\). Repeated integration by parts gives \(\int_0^1t^{r-\rho-1}(1-t)^\rho dt =(r-\rho-1)!\rho!/r!\). For \(\rho=r\), the count is \(\binom{am+r-1}{r}\); for \(\rho=0\), it is \(\binom{m+r-1}{r}\). These give the same limit.

We spell out the corresponding regular-sequence count. If \(J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\), then \(J^d/J^{d+1}\) is free over \(R/J\) on the degree-\(d\) monomials in the \(f_i\). Here is an induction proof. For \(I'=(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})\), the induction hypothesis gives the same description of its graded pieces. Since \(f_r\) is regular on \(R/I'\), it is regular on each such piece and hence on \(R/I'^m\). It follows that \((I'^m:f_r)=I'^m\). Expanding \(J^{m+1}=\sum_jf_r^jI'^{m+1-j}\) then gives \((J^{m+1}:f_r)=J^m\). To prove independence of the degree-\(d\) monomials, reduce a relation modulo \(f_r\). The induction hypothesis for the regular sequence in \(R/(f_r)\) puts the coefficients of the terms without \(f_r\) in \(J\). Remove these terms, divide the remainder by \(f_r\), and use the colon identity and induction on \(d\). All coefficients lie in \(J\). Permutation of a regular sequence in a local ring is the proved Proposition 1.2 of Regular sequences, depth and Cohen–Macaulay modules. The base case is cancellation of a nonzerodivisor.

Adding the graded lengths gives

\[ \operatorname{length}(R/J^m) =\binom{m+r-1}{r}\operatorname{length}(R/J). \tag{22.615} \]

Since \(J^m\subset I^m\), this is at least \(N_m\). Divide by \(m^r/r!\) and use (22.614) to prove (22.612). \(\square\)

Theorem 22.207. A multiplicity estimate from powers

Use the notation and hypotheses of Theorem 22.159, so that a nonzero section of multidegree \(L\) vanishes to order at least \(nT+1\) along \(W\) on \(\Sigma(n)\). There is a connected proper subgroup \(H\), of codimension \(r\), such that, with \(\rho=\dim W-\dim(W\cap\operatorname{Lie}H)\),

\[ (T+1)^\rho\,\#\{s+H:s\in\Sigma\}\, \mathcal H_H(L) \le2^{r-1}\mathcal H_G(L). \tag{22.616} \]

Proof. Repeat the ideal chain and the finite-coset construction of Theorem 22.159 through (22.439), keeping the ideal \(\mathcal J\) and its coset components rather than the numerical length bound. Choose \(v_0\in V\), and replace \(\mathcal J\) by \(t_{-v_0}^*\mathcal J\). This ideal contains the original section \(P\): the summand with translation \(v_0\) contains \(t_{v_0}^*P\).
